The question involves two simultaneous classifications used in the organization of health systems (particularly in the Brazilian SUS) and in preventive medicine.

Levels of health care complexity are defined as follows:
- Primary care corresponds to the scope of the family-and-community physician (health promotion, longitudinal follow-up, first-contact care).
- Secondary care corresponds to specialized ambulatory services that require intermediate technological density (e.g., an outpatient consultation with a cardiologist).
- Tertiary care is reserved for high-complexity, high-technology hospital procedures (cardiac surgery, advanced hemodynamic interventions, etc.).

The patient is being referred by his family physician to a cardiologist for specialized advice; therefore the encounter occurs at the secondary level of care.

Levels of prevention (Leavell & Clark) are defined as follows:
- Primary prevention – actions that prevent the first occurrence of disease.
- Secondary prevention – early detection plus prompt treatment aimed at limiting disability and preventing recurrence or progression once the disease is already present.
- Tertiary prevention – rehabilitation after sequelae have become established.

The patient already carries a diagnosis of ischemic heart disease and has suffered an acute myocardial infarction three months earlier. The anti-platelet regimen under discussion is precisely the set of measures classically labelled “secondary prevention” after an acute coronary syndrome (prevention of a new ischemic event and limitation of further myocardial damage). It is not primary (the disease has already declared itself) nor merely rehabilitative (tertiary).

Consequently the patient is seen at the secondary level of care and receives secondary prevention.

Final answer: B

- D is incorrect because confirmation of disease requires high specificity, not high sensitivity.

The infant presents with infantile spasms (flexor spasms occurring in clusters during drowsiness), developmental delay (inability to sit unsupported at 9 months), hypomelanotic macules, and MRI evidence of subependymal giant-cell astrocytomas. These four findings constitute major diagnostic criteria for tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).  

- Hypomelanotic (“ash-leaf”) macules are the most common cutaneous manifestation of TSC and are already visible in infancy.  
- Infantile spasms are the classic seizure type associated with TSC in the first year of life.  
- Subependymal giant-cell astrocytomas are virtually pathognomonic of TSC.  

The remaining options can be excluded on clinical and imaging grounds:  
- Neurofibromatosis type 1 features café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, not hypomelanotic macules or SEGAs.  
- Sturge–Weber syndrome is defined by a facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal angiomatosis.  
- von Hippel–Lindau disease presents later in life with cerebellar/retinal hemangioblastomas and visceral tumors, never with the neonatal/infantile phenotype described here.  

Thus the single diagnosis that unifies all of the findings is tuberous sclerosis (esclerose tuberosa).  

Final answer: B
